content:
**Progress M-14M (Progress 46P)** was a Russian uncrewed cargo spacecraft launched to resupply the **International Space Station (ISS)**. Here’s everything known about it:

---

### **1. Mission Overview**
- **Spacecraft Type:** Progress-M (11F615A60)
- **Manufacturer:** RSC Energia (Russia)
- **Launch Date:** **January 25, 2012, 23:06 UTC**
- **Launch Vehicle:** **Soyuz-U** (from **Baikonur Cosmodrome, Site 1/5**)
- **Docking Date:** **January 28, 2012, 00:09 UTC**
- **Docking Port:** **Pirs module (ISS)**
- **Undocking Date:** **April 19, 2012, 11:04 UTC**
- **Deorbit & Reentry:** **April 28, 2012** (burned up over the Pacific Ocean)

---

### **2. Payload & Cargo**
Progress M-14M carried **2,669 kg (5,884 lbs)** of supplies to the ISS, including:
- **Dry Cargo (1,260 kg):**
  - Food, clothing, and hygiene items for the crew.
  - Scientific equipment and experiments.
  - Spare parts and maintenance tools.
- **Propellant (880 kg):**
  - Fuel for ISS reboost maneuvers.
- **Water (420 kg):**
  - Fresh water for the crew.
- **Oxygen & Air (50 kg):**
  - Atmospheric gases for the station.

---

### **3. Mission Timeline**
- **Launch (Jan 25, 2012):**
  - Lifted off from Baikonur Cosmodrome on a Soyuz-U rocket.
  - Entered a **2-day rendezvous trajectory** (standard for Progress missions at the time).
- **Docking (Jan 28, 2012):**
  - Automatically docked to the **Pirs module** using the **Kurs automated rendezvous system**.
  - Expedition 30 crew (Dan Burbank, Anton Shkaplerov, Anatoli Ivanishin) monitored the approach.
- **Undocking (Apr 19, 2012):**
  - Filled with trash and waste from the ISS.
  - Undocked and moved to a safe distance for **Radar-Progress experiment** (studied plasma in the ionosphere).
- **Deorbit (Apr 28, 2012):**
  - Conducted a **deorbit burn** and reentered the atmosphere over the **South Pacific Ocean** (a standard disposal zone for Russian spacecraft).

---

### **4. Key Features of Progress M-14M**
- **Automated Docking:** Used the **Kurs-NA** (upgraded Kurs system) for rendezvous and docking.
- **Reboost Capability:** Could adjust the ISS’s orbit using its engines.
- **Disposable Design:** Unlike Soyuz, Progress spacecraft are not reusable and burn up on reentry.
- **Serial Number:** **M-14M** (also designated **Progress 46P** in NASA’s numbering system).

---

### **5. ISS Expedition Context**
- **Expedition 30 (Dec 2011 – Apr 2012):**
  - Crew: **Dan Burbank (NASA), Anton Shkaplerov (Roscosmos), Anatoli Ivanishin (Roscosmos)** (later joined by **Oleg Kononenko, André Kuipers, and Don Pettit**).
  - Progress M-14M was the **first resupply mission** of 2012 for the ISS.
- **Follow-up Missions:**
  - **Progress M-15M** (April 2012) – Next resupply flight.
  - **SpaceX Dragon (COTS Demo Flight 2)** – First commercial cargo mission (May 2012).

---

### **6. Technical Specifications**
| **Parameter**               | **Details** |
|-----------------------------|------------|
| **Spacecraft Mass**         | ~7,290 kg (at launch) |
| **Cargo Capacity**          | ~2,600 kg |
| **Length**                  | 7.23 m |
| **Diameter**                | 2.72 m |
| **Solar Panels Span**       | 10.6 m |
| **Propulsion**              | KTDU-80 (main engine) + 28 thrusters |
| **Power Supply**            | Solar panels + batteries |
| **Docking System**          | SSVP (Standard Probe-and-Cone) |

---

### **7. Notable Events & Experiments**
- **Radar-Progress Experiment:**
  - After undocking, Progress M-14M was used to study **plasma formations** in the ionosphere caused by engine firings.
  - Conducted by **Russian Academy of Sciences** and **Roscosmos**.
- **ISS Reboost:**
  - Used its engines to adjust the station’s orbit (a routine but critical function).

---

### **8. Comparison with Other Progress Missions**
- **Progress M-14M** was part of the **Progress-M** series (1989–2015), which succeeded the original Progress (1978–1990) and preceded the **Progress-MS** (2015–present).
- Unlike later **Progress-MS** spacecraft, M-14M lacked:
  - **Enhanced Kurs-NA** (though it used an earlier version).
  - **Digital flight control** (Progress-MS introduced this).
  - **Improved micrometeoroid shielding**.

---

### **9. Legacy & Impact**
- **Routine but Critical:** Progress M-14M was one of **~160 Progress missions** (as of 2024), demonstrating Russia’s reliable cargo delivery system.
- **International Collaboration:** Part of the **ISS resupply chain**, alongside NASA’s **SpaceX Dragon**, **Northrop Grumman Cygnus**, and **JAXA’s HTV**.
- **Predecessor to Progress-MS:** Helped pave the way for the modernized **Progress-MS** series, which began in 2015.

---

### **10. Media & Documentation**
- **NASA TV Coverage:** Docking and undocking were broadcast live.
- **Roscosmos Press Releases:** Provided mission updates (in Russian).
- **Photos & Videos:**
  - [NASA’s Progress M-14M Gallery](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/structure/elements/progress.html)
  - [Roscosmos Archive](https://www.roscosmos.ru/)

---

### **11. Fun Facts**
- **Name Confusion:** In NASA’s numbering system, it was **Progress 46P** (46th Progress to the ISS), while Russia used **M-14M** (14th in the M-series).
- **No Return Cargo:** Unlike SpaceX’s Dragon, Progress cannot return cargo to Earth—it burns up on reentry.
- **Fast Rendezvous Later:** Future Progress missions (after 2012) adopted a **6-hour fast rendezvous** instead of the 2-day approach.

---

### **12. Sources & Further Reading**
- [NASA ISS Resupply Missions](https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/structure/elements/progress.html)
- [Roscosmos Progress Missions](https://www.roscosmos.ru/)
- [Spaceflight101 – Progress M-14M](https://spaceflight101.com/progress-m-14m/)
- [Gunter’s Space Page – Progress M-14M](https://space.skyrocket.de/doc_sdat/progress-m.htm)
